title: Preregistered Paired Evaluation of a Deterministic Verifier Pipeline for LLM‑Generated Network Configuration Changes — Non‑informative Result under Shared‑Generation Semantics
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, archived paired experiment that asked whether a deterministic verifier pipeline (generate → deterministic_netops_validator_v5 → optional repair) reduces the rate of verifier‑detected unsafe intent→configuration proposals produced by a hosted LLM on synthetic NetOps tasks. Design: N=200 preregistered unique tasks in a paired design comparing (a) baseline LLM‑only and (b) guarded pipeline (gpt‑5‑mini + deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Execution used shared_initial_candidate generation semantics (independent_condition_generation = false), producing one LLM generation per task (model_calls_used = 200; preregistered maximum_model_calls = 400; completed_episode_count = 400; failed_episode_count = 0). Observed (adversarial cluster): baseline SAFE = 200/200; guarded SAFE = 200/200 (paired contingency n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0). Estimated paired SAFE‑rate difference = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (resamples = 10000, seed = 1729). Because identical per‑pair generations were produced and the observed baseline unsafe rate was 0%, the preregistered causal hypothesis (that a verifier reduces unsafe proposals) was not testable in this run. We publish the complete preregistered run and artifacts, provide an artifact‑grounded diagnosis of testability failure, and give concrete, archive‑supported recommendations (independent per‑arm generation, adversarial injection fraction, and model‑call budgeting) for informative repeats. All execution and analysis artifacts cited here are archived (execution/*, analysis/*).

sections.introduction:
Automating intent→configuration translation with large language models (LLMs) offers operator productivity gains for network operations (NetOps) but raises operational safety risks: an incorrect or ill‑timed change can break reachability, violate policy, or cause outages. Recent work therefore advocates tool‑grounding, deterministic validators, and generate–validate–repair architectures to improve correctness and reduce hallucination‑driven errors (see related work). Motivated by those proposals and by calls for workflow‑centred evaluation, we preregistered a confirmatory paired experiment (cand‑2026‑01‑prereg‑v1) to measure whether deterministic verifier augmentation reduces the rate of verifier‑detected unsafe configuration proposals from a hosted LLM under benign and adversarial prompts.

This paper reports the complete archived run, explains why the preregistered causal test was non‑informative in the executed configuration, and documents concrete, artifact‑grounded recommendations to make future repeats informative. Our research question (from the preregistration) was: How does deterministic tool‑augmentation (generate → deterministic validator → optional repair) change the rate of unsafe network‑change proposals produced by a hosted LLM under benign and adversarial NetOps prompts? Our contributions are threefold: (1) a fully preregistered, archived paired experiment comparing an LLM baseline and a deterministic verifier‑augmented pipeline on N=200 synthetic NetOps tasks with deterministic scoring and archived traces; (2) an artifact‑grounded diagnosis of why the confirmatory test yielded no discordant pairs (a ceiling/testability failure caused by shared generation semantics and a zero baseline unsafe rate); and (3) concrete, reproducible recommendations (independent per‑arm generation, adversarial injection budgeting, and model‑call accounting) supported by the archived execution and analysis artifacts.
sections.related_work:
Surveys and prototype reports show substantial interest in LLMs for NetOps tasks such as intent translation, configuration synthesis, and automated remediation. Recent overviews and prototypes document architectures that combine LLMs with deterministic tools or verifiers to improve measured correctness on curated tasks (e.g., tool‑augmented agent proposals and generate–validate–repair pipelines) [https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.12729; https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7132138; https://doi.org/10.1109/ojcoms.2026.3680457]. Complementary work on divide–verify–refine and self‑verification reports reductions in constraint violations, but effect sizes and generality depend on verifier fidelity, prompt design, and generation semantics [https://openalex.org/W4412888330; https://openalex.org/W7161354925].

Red‑teaming and guardrail literature emphasizes the safety/utility trade‑offs (false refusals versus unblocked unsafe proposals) and recommends workflow‑centred, replayable evaluations that include deterministic sandboxing and recorded traces. These methodological prescriptions motivated our preregistered design and the use of a deterministic sandboxed validator and archived scoring traces [https://doi.org/10.36227/techrxiv.177004277.71795055/v1; https://doi.org/10.36227/techrxiv.177006109.97957916/v1]. Our paper's novelty is methodological: we publish a complete confirmatory run and show how a specific execution choice—shared_initial_candidate generation semantics combined with limited model‑call budget—made the preregistered paired causal estimand untestable despite deterministic validation and complete archival.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. The study was preregistered as cand‑2026‑01‑prereg‑v1. The primary estimand was paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (SAFE encoded as 1). The design was a paired binary comparison with N=200 unique tasks (paired across two pipelines), planned_episode_count = 400, and an exact McNemar two‑sided test implemented by paired_binary_analysis_v1. The preregistered bootstrap CI used 10000 resamples and seed = 1729 for paired bootstrap percentile intervals.

Task generation, adversarial templates, and sampling plan. A deterministic task generator (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5) produced 200 synthetic intent→configuration tasks under an RNG seed schedule (preregistered seed=42 and task seeds 1..200). Tasks targeted operationally meaningful changes limited to admin, mtu, and vlan fields across single‑AS, multi‑device topologies. The sampling plan grouped tasks into benign and adversarial clusters; adversarial prompts were constructed by templated obfuscation/negation transforms (preregistered) to increase the chance of unsafe proposals. The full task manifest is archived at execution/task_manifest.jsonl and representative payloads are included in execution/representative_tasks within the artifact bundle.

Pipelines, generation semantics, and budget. Two pipelines were compared: (a) baseline LLM‑only, and (b) guarded pipeline that passes the LLM candidate through deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and optionally a single automatic repair. The preregistration allowed two generation semantics: independent per‑arm generation (each arm receives an independent LLM call) or shared_initial_candidate (one LLM generation shared across arms). The executed run used shared_initial_candidate (independent_condition_generation = false). The declared model in execution/model_configuration.json is "gpt‑5‑mini"; model_calls_used in execution/execution_manifest.json = 200 while the preregistered maximum_model_calls allocated for independent per‑arm generation = 400. Choosing shared generation halved the actual model calls and directly affected causal testability because identical per‑pair candidates were scored in both arms.

Deterministic validator, scoring, and repairs. deterministic_netops_validator_v5 was executed in a deterministic sandbox and applied full_intent_constraint_validation rules to classify proposals as SAFE/UNSAFE and to produce detailed validation_before/after traces. For confirmatory episodes no automatic repairs were applied (repair_provider_trace = null in the sampled scoring JSONs). Scoring files (execution/scoring/*.json) contain normalized_configuration, parsed command counts, validator verdicts, and violation lists; these artifacts are central to the confirmatory outcome coding.

Analysis executor and exact tests. The analysis executor paired_binary_analysis_v1 assembled the 2×2 paired contingency table and computed an exact McNemar two‑sided p‑value. Paired bootstrap percentile CIs used 10000 resamples (seed = 1729). The analysis artifacts are archived (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/condition_summary.csv, analysis/results.json). Missingness and technical failures were handled per preregistered rules: automated retries up to one retry per failed model call, exclusions/replacements for contamination flags, and a stopping rule for >10% technical failures. In execution there were no technical failures and no exclusions (analysis/missingness_summary.csv reports zero failures).
sections.results:
Execution accounting and raw outcomes. The run completed planned_episode_count = 400 with failed_episode_count = 0 and model_calls_used = 200 (one shared initial generation per task); the preregistered maximum_model_calls for independent per‑arm generation would have been 400 (execution/execution_manifest.json; execution/model_configuration.json). The analysis condition summary (analysis/condition_summary.csv) records baseline SAFE successes = 200/200 and guarded SAFE successes = 200/200 (SAFE encoded as 1), yielding observed SAFE rates of 1.0 for both arms.

Paired contingency and inferential summary. The paired contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is guarded vs baseline (SAFE encoding): n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The paired SAFE‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (resamples = 10000, seed = 1729). These numeric values were produced by the preregistered analysis executor and are present in analysis/results.json and the CSV artifacts.

Representative diagnostic artifacts. Per‑task scoring JSONs show that the shared_initial_candidate content was identical for baseline and guarded arms in every inspected confirmatory example (examples: execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json, task-000001-guarded.json, etc.). Validator traces within those files report violation_count = 0 and valid = true in validation_before and validation_after blocks; no repair_provider_trace entries were recorded for the confirmatory episodes, confirming the guarded pipeline did not exercise repairs in this sample. The deterministic reconciliation artifact (analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json) confirms consistent episode accounting (complete_pair_count = 200, provider_call_audit host calls = 200, all deterministic checks passed).

Sensitivity and missingness. The preregistered missingness and retry procedures were not invoked: analysis/missingness_summary.csv reports zero failed episodes and zero exclusions. The exploratory reserve (up to 50 tasks) was unused in the confirmatory test; exploratory ROC estimation remains possible from archived exploratory runs but was not part of the confirmatory analysis reported here.
sections.discussion:
Why the confirmatory test was non‑informative. The preregistered causal estimand required per‑arm variability to detect verifier impact: discordant pairs (n10 or n01) are the only sources of evidence in McNemar’s paired test. Three artifact‑grounded facts combined to produce a ceiling/testability failure. (1) Generation semantics: independent_condition_generation = false (shared_initial_candidate) produced identical LLM candidates per pair, so any per‑pair discordance could only arise from post‑generation repair in the guarded arm; (2) Baseline safety: on the sampled tasks and under gpt‑5‑mini, generated candidates satisfied the deterministic validator so baseline unsafe rate was 0% (baseline SAFE = 200/200); (3) Budgeting: the executed model_calls_used = 200 consumed only one LLM call per task rather than the 400 calls required for independent per‑arm generation under the preregistered plan. The conjunction of identical candidate sharing and a 0% baseline unsafe rate yields n10 = n01 = 0 and a degenerate McNemar configuration (n11 = 200), producing p = 1.0 and CI [0.0,0.0]. All these points are verifiable in execution/model_configuration.json and execution/execution_manifest.json and in the analysis artifacts.

Implications for evaluation design in NetOps. The run demonstrates that preregistration options must be aligned with causal testability. If the objective is a paired causal comparison of verifier effect, independent per‑arm generation must be the default because it permits per‑arm variability. For our design, independent per‑arm generation requires ≈200 additional model calls (preregistered maximum_model_calls = 400 versus executed 200). If resource constraints make independent generation infeasible, alternative confirmatory estimands should be preregistered (e.g., repeated independent draws within a single arm to estimate absolute unsafe rates, or deterministic injection of adversarial unsafe candidates for a fixed fraction of tasks). The preregistration captured these trade‑offs and the design alternatives; our run shows the pragmatic consequences when the shared generation option is executed.

Concrete, artifact‑grounded recommendations for informative repeats. (1) Allocate independent per‑arm generation: for N=200 pairs this implies model_calls ≈ 400 to permit McNemar‑style paired tests to detect verifier‑induced discordance. (2) Increase adversarial coverage by preregistering and calibrating an injection fraction of explicitly unsafe templates (e.g., X% of tasks injected with templated obfuscations or direct unsafe patterns) so that baseline unsafe rates are nonzero under the target model; record the injection fraction in the preregistration. (3) Reserve and use the exploratory sample (up to 50 tasks in our preregistration) to estimate verifier ROC (true positives and false positives) and report CIs. (4) Where budget allows, run a small multi‑model panel to assess generality across model families. These recommendations directly follow from the preregistration and execution accounting artifacts and are intended as actionable protocol changes to make future confirmatory comparisons informative.

Operational interpretation and cautious messaging. This run should not be read as empirical evidence that verifiers are unnecessary or universally ineffective; instead it is a reproducible methodological artifact that demonstrates how an otherwise well‑specified paired experiment can become untestable because of generation semantics and budgeting. We therefore frame the paper’s primary contribution as reproducibility and evaluation methodology rather than as an efficacy claim about the verifier.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully archived, preregistered paired experiment comparing an LLM baseline and a deterministic verifier‑augmented pipeline on 200 synthetic NetOps tasks. Under executed shared_initial_candidate semantics and for the declared model (gpt‑5‑mini), both arms produced zero verifier‑detected unsafe proposals (paired difference = 0.0; p = 1.0). Because identical per‑pair generations were produced and the observed baseline unsafe rate was 0%, the preregistered causal hypothesis could not be meaningfully evaluated in this run. The scientific contribution is methodological and reproducibility‑oriented: (1) we publish a complete preregistered run with deterministic artifacts that permit exact replay; (2) we provide an artifact‑grounded diagnosis of why this execution was non‑informative for verifier efficacy; and (3) we provide concrete, archived recommendations (independent per‑arm generation, adversarial budgeting, model‑call accounting) to design informative repeats. The archived execution and analysis bundle (execution/* and analysis/*) is provided to support deterministic replays and community replication.

limitations: Synthetic tasks and scope: tasks were deterministic synthetic topologies limited to single‑AS, multi‑device setups produced by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5; results may not generalize to production, multi‑AS, or vendor‑specific features.

Generation semantics: the executed run used shared_initial_candidate (independent_condition_generation = false), producing identical per‑pair generations and creating a ceiling effect when shared candidates were valid.

Adversarial strength: the preregistered adversarial templates used in this run did not elicit unsafe outputs from gpt‑5‑mini on the sampled tasks; stronger adversarial cases or injected unsafe examples are required to measure verifier effect.
Single‑model scope: only the declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) was evaluated; no multi‑model generality is claimed.

Verifier completeness: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 ran deterministically in synthetic sandboxed states; external validation of validator completeness against all real‑world NetOps failure modes is not provided.

Operational external validity: no production deployment, operator‑in‑the‑loop workload measurement, nor multi‑vendor field trials were performed; operator‑cost trade‑offs remain unquantified at scale.
